articles.text: Thousands of people from Piedmont and beyond are expected to converge near Piedmont Park on November 24 for the 21st annual Turkey Trot. The 5-kilometer race will begin at 8:30 a.m. The popular Thanksgiving morning event is celebrating its 21st year. Runners, joggers. Dog walkers and families with strollers will gather on Highland Avenue in front of the Exedra at the corner of Highland and Magnolia Avenues. Coffee and hot chocolate will be served at Corcoran Group, formerly Highland Partners, at the beginning and the end of the race. There will also be plenty of refreshments afterwards. The race begins on Highland Avenue and continue onto Wildwood Avenue and La Salle Avenue, before looping back along Sea View and Mountain Avenues. The route is considered a good workout for serious runners and a benchmark for hundreds of others looking to improve their time or just get some morning exercise with a lot of friends and neighbors. Although anyone can join the race, those who have registered are in the running to win some sweet prizes. All registered runners should plan to pick up their race bib and official Piedmont Turkey Trot jersey on Wednesday, November 23 at the Veterans Hall between 3:00 and 5:00 p.m. Winners will be announced at an awards ceremony in front of the Exedra after the last runner crosses the finish line. Prizes are awarded to the top three runners in each age category, from youth to seniors over 80. All winners will receive a racing cap, a fresh bouquet of flowers from J. Miller Flowers, and a pumpkin pie from Piedmont Grocery. The overall male and female winners will receive a turkey from Village Market, and running shoes from Transports. Proceeds from the Turkey Trot support Piedmont High School cross country and track-and-field teams and the City of Piedmont’s sorts facilities maintenance fund.

articles.text: At a Special City Council Meeting on Tuesday, November 15, Piedmont’s city staff received council authorization to submit Piedmont’s Draft Housing Element, with several proposed updates, to the California Department of Housing and Community Development. The updates include: • maximizing the use of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) from 140 to 160 to meet State-mandated housing production targets • relocation of affordable units in the housing sites inventory from the Civic Center area to the mixed-use zone on Grand Avenue • keeping Above Moderate Income units on Grand Avenue at or below five stories • expanding the Moraga Canyon Plan area to include all cityowned property along Moraga Avenue, including Blair Park. Each city in California has an allocated Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) number, which specifies the target number of homes to plan for at various income levels. Piedmont’s housing target is 587 units. This includes 163 Very Low Income units, 94 Low Income units, 92 Moderate Income units, and 238 Above Moderate Income units. California law requires cities to update their Housing Element every eight years. articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department invites community members to donate toys for children whose families have trouble affording holiday gifts as part of the 75th Anniversary Toys for Tots Donation Drive. Donations of new, unwrapped toys may be dropped off at the Piedmont Fire Department during regular business hours now through December 9. Donation bins are located in the Fire Department adjacent to City Hall at 120 Vista Avenue. “The Piedmont Fire Department is proud to partner with the Alameda County Marine Toys for Tots Foundation,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Every year the generosity of the Piedmont community brings hope and joy to children throughout Alameda County.” In a longstanding tradition, each member of the Piedmont City Council will donate a toy to the Toys for Tots program. Their donations will take place at the December 5 council meeting in City Hall. The Toys for Tots Foundation, a not-for-profit public charity, is sponsored by the U. S. Marine Corps Reserve. For more information on donating a toy in Piedmont, please contact Fire Captain Jon Fitzpatrick at (510) 420-3030 (jfitzpatrick@piedmont.ca.gov).

articles.text: Bring back the original 19th century Blair Park Editor: Blair Park, along Moraga Ave, is a perfect place for high density housing. The site is easily accessible for developers. Everyone who drives on Moraga Ave, past Blair Park knows that it is very underused. Who wants to be in a park with such heavy traffic speeding past? Please move the new Blair Park from its current 4.85 acre location in Moraga Canyon. The park, not housing, would be better located on a portion of the original 75 acre Blair Park site, above Coaches Field-high on the hillside (see historyofpiedmont. com search Blair Park)! All Piedmont residents could enjoy this superior park location high on the hill with its mature trees, some of the original graded trails, and unsurpassed views. Following is a description of our magnificent hillside from the San Francisco Morning Call newspaper, dated Sunday, March 22, 1891. Page 8: “a splendid view is had over the whole Bay Area, that ranges from the Golden from Berkeley to Alameda on this shore and from Mount Tamalpias down along the Coast Range” Isn’t it better for our climate issues if Piedmonters just walk out of their houses to a majestic new Blair Park on the mountain for exercise, rather than jumping into their cars to drive somewhere else? It was a highly desired destination for people in 1891 and it could be again. Pictured are: (front) Carter Brookfield (left), Gus Leonard, Henry Stein, Theo Ferguson; (standing on truck) Will Myers, Colin Amen, Zach Osborn, and Drew Kobal. Piedmont Council Scouts stepped up on Saturday, November 12 in its 38th annual Scouting for Food drive, providing support for the Alameda County Community Food Bank and the people it serves. “Alameda County has one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation,” said Anne Hauss Davies, Piedmont Scout Council’s Scouting for Food Chair. “One of every five residents of the County calls upon the Alameda Food Bank for assistance, and two-thirds of those requiring assistance are children and the elderly. More than half of those served by the Food Bank have jobs but aren’t earning enough to make ends meet.” The service project, done by Scouts across the nation for decades, incorporates Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, and Venturers. The prior weekend, November 5, Cub Scouts distributed door hangers reminding Piedmont residents to place donations of non-perishable outside. Piedmont Scouts followed up last weekend throughout the city to pick up the donations and bring them to the parking lot at Piedmont Community Hall where Venturers from the Piedmont Community Service Crew helped sort the donations and load them onto a truck from the food bank. “It’s a huge lift, but it’s made lighter because so many people step in and step up,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “This wouldn’t happen without the generosity of the greater Piedmont community.” Each Pack and Troop’s route was mapped out in advance for both the door hangers and food pickup. One of this year’s highlights was Troop 4’s coordinator Kevin Blodgett. “Kevin is a recent Eagle Scout,” said Benson, “and it’s great to see him continuing to lead in his troop.” In a sign of the community’s generosity, the truck was fully loaded with donations when it left for the Food Bank. Scouts also brought in over $3,000 in cash and checks and the virtual food drive raised an additional $6,000 as of November 14. Scouting in Piedmont Are you interested in Scouting for your family? Programs are available for youth in grade school (Cub Scouts), youth 11-18 (Scouts BSA), and youth 14-21 (Venturing and Exploring). Piedmont responds with generosity to annual Scouting for Food drive Piedmont Council Scouts stepped up on Saturday, November 12 in its 38th annual Scouting for Food drive, providing support for the Alameda County Community Food Bank and the people it serves. “Alameda County has one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation,” said Anne Hauss Davies, Piedmont Scout Council’s Scouting for Food Chair. “One of every five residents of the County calls upon the Alameda Food Bank for assistance, and two-thirds of those requiring assistance are children and the elderly. More than half of those served by the Food Bank have jobs but aren’t earning enough to make ends meet.” The service project, done by Scouts across the nation for decades, incorporates Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, and Venturers. The prior weekend, November 5, Cub Scouts distributed door hangers reminding Piedmont residents to place donations of non-perishable outside. Piedmont Scouts followed up last weekend throughout the city to pick up the donations and bring them to the parking lot at Piedmont Community Hall where Venturers from the Piedmont Community Service Crew helped sort the donations and load them onto a truck from the food bank. “It’s a huge lift, but it’s made lighter because so many people step in and step up,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “This wouldn’t happen without the generosity of the greater Piedmont community.” Each Pack and Troop’s route was mapped out in advance for both the door hangers and food pickup. One of this year’s highlights was Troop 4’s coordinator Kevin Blodgett. “Kevin is a recent Eagle Scout,” said Benson, “and it’s great to see him continuing to lead in his troop.” In a sign of the community’s generosity, the truck was fully loaded with donations when it left for the Food Bank. Scouts also brought in over $3,000 in cash and checks and the virtual food drive raised an additional $6,000 as of November 14. Scouting in Piedmont Are you interested in Scouting for your family? articles.text: Symphony horn players will be returning to the Piedmont Turkey Trot again this year on Thanksgiving morning starting at 8 a.m. for a festive fanfare that officially launches the race in the middle of town. Last year’s musicians included Tom Reicher(left), Berkeley Symphony; Stuart Gronningen, Oakland Symphony (retired); Alicia Mastromonaco, Marin Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, Santa Cruz Symphony; Meredith Brown, Oakland Symphony; Jonathan Ring, San Francisco Symphony; and Robert Ward, San Francisco Symphony. They will be joined this year by an eighth brass player, Daniel Hawkins of San Francisco Symphony. “We will have eight hunting horn players who will be playing on authentic trompes de chasse from France,” explained Piedmont resident Tom Reicher, a French Horn player with Berkeley Symphony. “Originally, the trompe de chasse was used as a loud signaling instrument that would communicate to hunters various aspects of the hunt. However, over more than two centuries music was developed for large ensembles of trompes de chasse, and that is what we will be playing. This is music intended to be performed outdoors and thus is appropriate to celebrate the gathering of runners for the Piedmont Turkey Trot.”

articles.text: Due to California’s ongoing school funding crisis, many school districts have cut the hours of their libraries or closed them altogether. Thanks to the Piedmont community’s support of the Giving Campaign, Piedmont’s libraries are stronger than ever, serving as hubs of literacy, interactive learning, and connection for students. These active, multi-faceted spaces and the librarians and aides that run them depend in large part on support from the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) and its Giving Campaign. At every Piedmont school, dedicated teacher librarians and aides help students develop a love of reading along with critical thinking and research skills. A significant portion of the funding for aides in the libraries comes from funds raised by the Giving Campaign. “The tri-school elementary teacher librarians are so grateful to PEF for its ongoing library funding,” said Havens Elementary teacher librarian Laura Remer. “We couldn’t do our work without having the support of our library assistants. They take care of some of the nitty gritty so that we can focus on teaching and helping our students find just-right books for their reading level, for their personal interests, and for supporting who they are as individuals.” Beyond encouraging a love of reading, school libraries and librarians provide students with the tools they need to develop critical thinking skills and media literacy. In a recent middle school project led by teacher librarians Jennifer Gulassa and Carolyn White, students selected one Amendment from the Bill of Rights. Using online databases, they researched and read three news articles about current events and considered how they impacted their chosen amendment. “This project helped students understand how our founding documents still impact current events and their own lives,” said Gulassa. “It integrated the use of key words for database searches, citations, extraction of key ideas, reflection, and collaboration.” Piedmont school libraries also serve as calm spaces for students during lunch hour. When previous library staff members retired, the school district lacked the budget to replace them, so all three elementary schools were forced to close their libraries during the lunch hour. Last year’s Giving Campaign prioritized funds for library aides to allow the district to continue to offer students the respite and opportunities the libraries provide. With new funding, the district has reopened the libraries during the lunch hour. “We are so happy to now be able to serve our students nearly every recess of the week,” noted Remer. “We know that for some students a quiet space to relax, read, and do a variety of activities is important to their social-emotional well-being.” During lunch, elementary school library staff offer activities like Legos, puzzles, coloring, origami, board games, and chess. Havens library aide Christina Wagg knows firsthand the value of having a welcoming library in which to spend free time. “I lived in the Montclair library as a kiddo,” she says. Piedmont Middle School teacher librarians Carolyn White (left) and Jennifer Gulassa. “Going there every day after school, I knew I would always be welcome. It was a godsend for me.” Funds from the Giving Campaign cover 10%-15% of the costs of librarians at each school. “That funding is the difference between librarians being able to teach five versus six classes,” said PEF director Heather Frank. “Our librarians make these libraries into places kids want to come and learn.” Thanks to the Giving Campaign, Piedmont school libraries will continue to be a space for learning and growth. “I believe libraries are a safe haven for all, where we make connections, learn about our world, read, write, draw, create, and take a break from the busyness,” said Wagg. “I’m so glad the Piedmont community values its beautiful libraries.” To learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign or to donate, please visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org.
articles.title: School libraries a rich resource for Piedmont students

articles.text: Community members are invited to the new Alan Harvey theater tonight to contribute to the search for a permanent school superintendent. A public forum will be held tonight, Wednesday, November 16, at 6 p.m. allowing residents to provide input towards Piedmont School District’s search for a permanent school superintendent. The meeting will be held in the new Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus. Residents will have an opportunity to interact with consultants from the search firm, Leadership Associates, which has been hired by the school board to lead the search. Residents are asked to provide input about desired personal and professional qualities anticipated in the incoming superintendent. Comments from the public will be used in the development of the candidate profile, recruitment process, and reference checking. The consultants will compile a summary of all comments received and share the report with the School Board and with the future superintendent. “The search firm has a great reputation for finding excellent candidates for school districts,” said Interim Superintendent Donald Evans. “You can’t create the candidate profile without listening to the Piedmont community. Piedmont is about relationships. They have to be involved and engaged in the process. This is how parents stay connected to the superintendent search.” During the forum, consultants will share an overview of the process, and ask audience members the following questions: • What are the desirable qualities, characteristics, background and professional and personal experiences for the next superintendent? • What do you see as the strengths of the district and the major challenges facing the district in years ahead? There is no need to RSVP. Those unable to attend may provide feedback and responses to these questions on an online survey at: Surveymonkey.com/r/53FDH9S. The survey will remain open until November 21 at 4:00 p.m.

articles.text: This year Piedmont and Millennium High School are offering a new class, Affinity Mentorship, after school hours in the 8th period. A total of 36 high school mentors have enrolled in the diversity-focused course which aims to make an impact on middle and elementary school students in Piedmont schools. The class trains high school students to create effective and age-appropriate lessons on identity. The mentors put their work into action by offering mentoring sessions to younger students of similar cultural, ethnic, religious, gender-expansive, and neurodiverse backgrounds. Neurodiverse is an umbrella term that includes people with autism, dyslexia, ADHD, or other neurological differences resulting in varying perspectives of the world. Mentors meet with their students two to three times each month creating fun, safe spaces for young mentees to explore and celebrate their identities. The Affinity Mentorship program has seen growth since it began in 2020, allowing mentors to expand services to middle school students. This year also brought the capability to deliver sessions to the district’s neurodiverse and gender-expansive Photo by Jean Takazawa Sage Mosley (left), and Julia Banuelos (right) with 3rd graders Isaac Pelletier and Ramon Fierro. students. “To be able to recognize that there are students, neurodivergent students, and gender expansive students that would really benefit from actually having mentors in those identities, has been really amazing for the younger students,” said Jean Takazawa, who teaches the Affinity Mentorship class. “I didn’t know it was going to go this far. I am so glad it got approved,” said senior Sage Mosley, one of the original founders of the program and Co-President of the Black Student Union. Photo by Jean Takazawa Stephine and Natalie Tsung mentor 1st grader Ethan Hong, 2nd grader Eli Kan-Miller, and 3rd grader Ellie Hong. While the other four student founders have graduated, the original motivation continues, “We wanted to do this because there are a lot of kids who look like us and don’t feel safe in an environment here at Piedmont,” added Mosley. Addy Neel, a two-year Affinity Mentor and Black Student Union Co-President, said, “A lot of kids have had a lot of experiences of racism because I feel like African American kids do get it more. And so we come together, we talk about these experiences, and we bring it to the school. We let the students know that they are able to talk in this safe space and don’t have to be afraid to show emotion or speak up.” Neel also expressed the importance of a program like this in Piedmont. “Piedmont is predominantly white, with many very wealthy people who may not really be exposed to a lot of diversity. Because of that, inappropriate things get said. Many Piedmonters do not know how to interact with people that are different. This class allows us a space to talk about our differences,” Neel added. To know more or if interested in signing your child up for the class, see: drive.google.com/ file/d/1oyRio8o8kEAMB_yCuBNuoz2r vl m A6929/view?usp=sharing.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont coach Dan Chubbock and the girls’ soccer team return with a roster that includes 10 seniors. Piedmont girls’ soccer coach can hardly wait for the winter season to begin. His team includes 10 seniors and five other players who earned varsity time last year. “We have a lot of returning players and a couple of freshmen; there’s a lot of familiarity across the board and returning cohesion. There’s a lot of competition for places, so there’s a lot of good headaches at each position,” he said. “We had our first practice since tryouts and everyone looks good. Starting with the attack, fouryear starter Emily Fitzgerald and two-year starter Audrey Lam are back in the fold. For Emily, she’s an even stronger player than last year and will have a big impact on the league,” said Chubbock. Last year’s striker Zenobia Pellissier-Lloyd is likely to be replaced on the front line by Fitzgerald and possibly freshman Miranda Liu. “Miranda Liu is a center forward by trade, and she’ll be fighting for a spot. I think we’ll be stronger going forward this year. Miranda can fill that striker role; the same for Emily,” he added. On defense, Piedmont returns a group of center backs who saw a lot of action last season: Sofie Hebert, Charlotte Davis, Elle Ruegg, Audrey Harmon, and Amy Derr. Eliza Hammond, a JV call-up, has been impressive this offseason. “There’s definitely competition at center back. Honestly we have two or three options at every position this year, which is great,” said Chubbock. With the amount of returners, PHS s likely to have a balanced team in all phases of the game. “I think it’s a strong team this year. articles.text: Piedmont enters season as defending NCS Champion Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team comes into the upcoming Winter season as the defending Division 4 North Coast Section champions and winning the WACC’s Shoreline Division with undefeated records for two years. The high-level results have earned the Highlanders a promotion to the WACC’s Foothill Division. “This is for sure going to be a transition year. We’ve had a lot of success over the last three years and were able to cap it off in the right fashion by winning NCS. But with success comes new challenges. Being moved up into the [more competitive] Foothill Division will be a huge challenge,” said coach Todd Sullivan. With the loss of 14 seniors from last year’s team, Sullivan is forced Aiden Woolwine, the Post’s 2022 Honorable Mention for Sophomore of the Year, is back to lead the front line. Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team returns as the defending Division 4 NCS champions and have been moved up to the WACC Foothill Division. to replace several key starters, including former captain and midfielder Andre Stankiewicz, forward Conner Curtis, center back Ian Work, and winger Russell Tan, currently in Spain with Atletico Madrid’s Academy. Last year, Piedmont defeated Bishop O’Dowd 1-0 and San Leandro 2-0 but lost narrowly 1-0 to Castro Valley and Berkeley. “Playing the likes to Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, San Leandro, and Castro Valley twice in a season will definitely take a toll on our record. It’s going to be important to focus on our Div. 4 games to clinch a playoff position,” said Sullivan. Sullivan’s attack is characterized by a possessive style, high pressing, and keeping the ball in the opponent’s half. With the large amount of changes to the roster, he expects a more direct style that utilizes their speed and athleticism. Three-year starter Aiden Woolwine, will be back to lead the front line. “The style of play may be tweaked as a result of the changes. We likely won’t play the attractive brand of soccer that we’ve been used to seeing, but we’ll still be a high intensity pressing team that looks to keep the tempo high. We’ll have a more direct attack this year and we have a few pacey players who can go up there, like Sam Shelby and Jack Zirkelbach is quick as well,” said Sullivan. Piedmont will still be able to have a solid defense with returning starters goalkeeper Daniel Malecki, fullback Evan Manolis, and center back Soren Dixon. “We still have a decent amount of starters from last year that make up the defensive shape. There’s still continuity there and then we have to figure out how to build around that. Miles Corcoron is a good center back, Andrew Szerdy is another one and he’s a big boy, so we have some options,” said Sullivan. Moving to the midfield, Piedmont will have to replace last year’s captain, Stankiewicz, which is no easy task. Inheriting the captain’s armband will be fellow midfielder T.J. O’Neil, who earned a first-team All-League selection last season. “T.J. is going to be our mainstay, he’s a big part of the team this year and we’ll be able to build around him in the midfield. We have a couple of other good players on the ball. We’ll miss Andre’s energy and presence on the ball. Will Daniel is someone who can get some time in the midfield as well,” said Sullivan. Piedmont opens its season tonight, Wednesday, November 16 with a 7:00 p.m. game at Oakland Tech.

Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team will open its season with five seniors and six juniors, a roster coach Ben Spencer calls his largest sized group in his four years at the helm. In addition to their height and heft, Spencer expects it to be his deepest team in several years, with at least nine players who will regularly contribute. The Highlanders posted a 17-11 record last season and advance to the Div. 3 North Coast Section semifinals as the No. 3 seed before losing by two points to No. 2 Branson. “Last year, we had six losses that were three-points or less. The last three years we’ve been really successful and we have a chance to be really good again. This could be our best and deepest team since winning the NCS Championship in 2020. It’s the biggest and most skilled team I’ve had,” said Spencer. Coming back as a leader is 6-foot-5 senior forward A.J. Harris. He was vocal leader of the team throughout the summer and offseason program, getting teammates in the gym to train. He’s on target to join the school’s 1,000 career point club this season. Junior Brit Burden, also 6-feet, 5-inches, has been a main figure in the offseason program. “A.J. and Brit have been setting that culture. They are lifting weights on the weekends and making sure players show up at shootarounds. When we couldn’t get gym time, Brit and A.J. were getting guys to go to the Oakland YMCA at 6 a.m. It feels like one big family, which is great going into the season,” said Spencer. Piedmont will be without JoJo Murphy, now a freshman on Chico State’s basketball team. Harris (left) is set to be Piedmont’s next 1,000 career point scorer. guard who is replacing JoJo. He has big shoes to fill as our point guard replacing JoJo. He has a lot of length and is a really good defender. He got a lot of minutes on JV and I think he’ll surprise some people,” said Spencer. Theo Evans is another returning senior who got minutes last season. The shooting guard will have a larger role this year, and Spencer thinks he’s up to the task. “He’s our third captain alongside A.J. and Brit. He’s a quiet leader who leads by example. He’s someone who can take us from being a good team to a great team. When Theo is making shots, we are incredibly hard to guard. When he’s sinking them, we can become a championship-level team. We basically played all of June and July in tournaments,” said Spencer. Guys were ready to get after it and we competed at Modesto Christian and the St. Mary’s Team Camp over the summer. articles.text: John Savage is a well respected and well liked chemistry teacher at Piedmont High School, his alma mater. He’s also a water polo coach at the school. He is also an accomplished triathlete who qualified this fall for the famed Ironman World Championship in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii. On Saturday, October 8, Savage finished in 538th overall out of 2,376 athletes, and placed 154th out of 419 athletes in the 35-39 age division. To qualify for the prestigious event, Savage raced in Ironman Texas on April 23, where he was fifth of 221 athletes in his age group, and 39th overall in a field of 2,273 triathletes. His race in Hawaii featured a 2.4 mile swim in Kailua Bay followed by a 112 mile bike course that had 5,814 feet of elevation gain, and finished with a 26.2 mile run, which included a total elevation gain of 1,009 feet. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California is drawing upon its extensive collection to feature the works of late Oakland-based artist Hung Liu, who passed away in August, 2021. The museum has regularly showcased Liu’s work during her lifetime, including during Women’s History Month alongside other famed female artists like Mine Okubo, Helen Nestor, and Favianna Rodriguez. The museum had a longstanding partnership with the artist and commissioned her installation at the Oakland Airport, Going Away, Coming Home. Oakland Museum is also featuring a survey of her works in the exhibition titled Summoning Ghosts: The Art of Hung Liu in 2013. That installation opened in October, 2021 and features four of Liu’s works in the Gallery of California Art: Still Point (1998), Heroine of Gu Yanxiu (2012), Bindlestiff (2015) and Portrait of Dorothea Lange (2017), inspired by photographs by the famous Depression Era photographer Lange. To learn more about the exhibition and artworks, visit https:// museumca.org/on-view/remembering-artist-hung-liu/.

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco has opened an exhibition titled The New Black Vanguard: Photography between Art and Fashion and will be on view through March 5, 2023. In its West Coast premiere, the exhibit highlights the work of 15 contemporary fashion photographers from London, Lagos, New York, Johannesburg, and beyond. Each artist’s work showcases a fresh perspective on fashion, beauty, race, gender, and aesthetics. The New Black Vanguard is curated by Antwaun Sargent and organized by Aperture, New York. Visitors will see over 100 select works from international artists and photographers, including Tyler Mitchell, the first Black photographer hired to shoot a cover story for American Vogue. To learn more and to purchase tickets to MoAD, visit https:// www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/thenew-black-vanguard. Photographs displayed in current exhibit at MoAD in San Francisco. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse will premiere a production of Shakespeare’s As You Like It tomorrow, November 17. The epic tale is adapted for stage by Shaina Taub and Laurie Woolery, and follows the same basic story, illustrated by eight characters who all marry at the end of the play. A major theme in Shakespeare’s classic is love – disguised, blind and even manipulated. Duke Senior and his followers are forced from their homes, then escape to the Forest of Arden where they are welcomed by a utopian vision of society. articles.text: Bay Area favorite James Carpenter returns in role of Ebeneezer Scrooge A Christmas Carol returns to San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater (ACT) on Wednesday, November 30 with performances through Christmas eve, December 24. The production stars Bay Area favorite James Carpenter as Ebeneezer Scrooge, a role strongly identified with him, and which he has performed with ACT for 15 years The play is based on Charles Dickens’ famous story that captures the zeitgeist of the mid-Victorian era, with main character Ebenezer Scrooge at its center. Dicken’s novella has been recounted onstage and in film for nearly a century; ACT’s production is adapted by Carey Perloff and Paul Walsh and directed by Peter Kuo. Music is scored by Karl Lundenberg with choreography by Val Caniparoli. The cast is once again led by James Carpenter, with Anthony Fusco in alternating performances as Ebenezer Scrooge. Dan Hiatt plays the Ghost of Jacob Marley, Jomar Tagatac and Sarita Ocón are cast as Bob and Anne Cratchit; Brian Herndon and Sharon Lockwood are Mr. and Mrs. Fezziwig; B Noel Thomas is the Ghost of Christmas Past; and Catherine Castellanos as the Ghost of Christmas Present. Also featured are Tasi Alabastro, John Chukwudelunzu, Evangeline Edwards, Steven Flores, Cindy Goldfield, Jeremy Kahn, Adam KuveNiemann, Paige Mayes, James WDL Mercer II, Emily Newsome, Amanda Le Nguyen, Anna Marie Sharpe, and Howard Swain. A Christmas Carol has been a mainstay of ACT’s repertory for decades. Performances will take place at the newly-named Toni Rembe Theater at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. The production uses theatrical haze and lighting that may not be appropriate for photosensitive groups. A sensory-friendly performance of A Christmas Carol will be performed on December 18 at 6 p.m. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ whats-on/202223-season/christmas-carol/ to purchase tickets. articles.text: “There’s good news“ is how a famous news program used to begin. These days all new sources except for the Piedmont Post tell us that it’s the bad news that sells. I don’t buy it…and apparently neither do the voters. They passed proposition 28 by a whopping majority. This proposition will increase the spending in California’s public schools for music and the arts. The public, in its wisdom, realizes that music and the arts are important. They are pledging about $1 billion in the hopes that society will benefit. It will, but I don’t trust the big shots in education. This subject requires an in-depth analysis which will follow very soon. Heard recently at the PCA The unique San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra played a delightful concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last Saturday afternoon. I arrived just in time to hear a Suite of compositions by one of the most unique figures in music history… a Frenchman by the name of Erik Satie. The featured soloist was the noted opera singer/narrator Twila Ehmcke. Satie always had a unique way of looking at everything. In this piece, he writes music for children; and as you might expect, his way of looking at things is very childish. He sees children as annoying even though he loves them. Needless to say, the audience loved it all. Violinists take over Orange County The Violin Society of America is hosting its 24th annual convention in Anaheim. It is fun to renew old friendships and begin new ones. Hundreds of violin makers are in attendance. In addition to technical workshops, there will be a number of concerts and some very important discussions involving ecological concerns. My taxi ride from the airport to the hotel was most informative. The taxi driver filled me in on all aspects of the area. It turns out that he is a knowledgeable gourmet, so he told me about the best restaurants. Southern California is quite different from Northern California as most of us know. The strip malls in Southern California have restaurants which actually feature good food. Little Arabia is a perfect example. Even though it is surrounded by corporate vapidness, I felt as if I were in Beirut, Lebanon. Service was excellent and friendly. The restaurant was filled with young families and well-mannered kids. I looked into the kitchen and saw the owner-chef busy at work. He has the grizzled face of culinary wisdom. My son and I shared a huge combo plate filled with flavorful and fragrant delicacies of the Middle East. It was so large that my son and I couldn’t finish it all. A brief conversation with the owner and the management convinced me that these people love what they are doing. People line up for workshops and concerts at the Violin Society of America’s 24th annual convention in Anaheim.

articles.text: Empire of the Sun, released in 1987 and directed by Steven Spielberg, is extraordinary. It was adapted by screenwriter Tom Stoppard from the autobiographical novel by J.G. Ballard, and earned six Oscar nominations at the 60th Academy Awards ceremony. It is a must-see classic that will appeal to a wide audience, from older kids to adults. Its moving score is by John Williams with a recurring thematic leitmotif solo by James Rainbird, backed by the Ambrosian Junior Choir. The story focuses on a young, privileged British boy, Jamie Graham (Christian Bale), who lives with his parents in a cloistered expat Shanghai community that is convinced it is immune from the gathering storm of World War II, until it isn’t. The Japanese invade Shanghai, and in a remarkable, surging scene, Jamie is separated from his parents. He suddenly finds himself surrounded by crowds of panicky Chinese. The last words he hears his mother yell at him as she is swept away by a surge of humanity, are to go home and wait. Which he does. His parents never return, and Christian Bale stars in Empire of the Sun. Jamie soon runs out of food. Desperate, he decides to bicycle to the urban center of Shanghai. Through a series of circumstances, involving two American expats, Basie and Frank (John Malkovich and Joe Pantolino), the three are captured and sent to a British prisoner of war camp where they are interned by the Japanese for the duration of the war. Jamie (called Jim by Basie) soon learns that if he is to survive the harsh conditions of the camp he must emulate Basie who has an array of side-hustles. He also learns that nothing in his Christian Bale and Takatarô Kataoka in a scene from Empire of the Sun. previous affluent, sheltered life prepared him for what he is now confronting. articles.text: Ewan McGregor with Winnie the Pooh in Christopher Robin. Christopher Robin is a live-action/animated fantasy film inspired by the books of A.A. Milne, replete with the iconic illustrations of E.H. Shepard. If I had to select an ideal age for this movie, I would pick tweens and early teens, despite the strong animated opening. The tale begins with a young Christopher Robin in the 100 Acre Woods with his friends, Winnie the Pooh, Piglet, Tigger et.al. The lad is about to leave for boarding school, and the gang is giving him a farewell tea party. Christopher comforts Winnie (Jim Cummings), reassuring the honey-loving bear that he will never forget him. And so begins the transition from animation to live-action. As it turns out, the boy has a difficult time in school. His father unexpectedly dies, and he soon puts the 100 Acre Woods behind him. He grows up (now played by Ewan McGregor), marries an architect, Evelyn (Hayley Atwell), has a daughter, Madeline (Bronte Carmichael), and serves in World War II. After the war, he finds a demanding job with Winslow Luggage Co. as an efficiency expert, working long hours while increasingly neglecting his family. In other words, Christopher is losing perspective, putting his work before everything else, including a promised family vacation. This commitment to his job takes the story to that one day when Christopher is sitting on a bench in London’s Langdon Park, staring off into the distance, feeling somewhat dejected when suddenly, on a bench behind him, appears the long-forgotten Pooh. And so, Winnie attempts to remind his old friend about what really matters. Initially, Christopher disagrees with the small bear, insisting that “there’s more to life than balloons and honey.” Pooh responds by asking, “Are you sure?” Meanwhile Christopher suggests that perhaps he should take Winnie back to the 100 Acre Woods, and so their adventure begins with Christopher hiding the bear under his coat hoping he won’t be seen by ordinary people. Along the way the pair confront the much-feared Heffalumps and the Woozles. All the while the pair exchange ideas as to how to keep Christopher’s luggage company afloat. Gradually, Christopher begins to recover his sense of joy and slowly realizes what is important in life. He reconnects with Pooh, who reminds him, “there’s always time for wonder.” Christopher Robin is a whimsical story, value-laden with a strong anti-bullying message, and conveys countless life-lessons about the strength of the human spirit. Older kids will be entertained by the seamless merging of real life action and CGI. Christopher Robin. Directed by Marc Forster. Starring Ewan McGregor, Jim Cummings, Haley Atwell. 1 hr., 44 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: Mitch Winters as a young boy receives a kiss from his younger sister, Elizabeth. A foundation was just launched to assist children of first responders in Alameda County. The foundation honors the memory of Mitch Winters, a Piedmont native and 2016 Piedmont High School graduate, who died by suicide one year ago in November 2021. Being a first responder (military personnel, law enforcement officers, firefighters, paramedics, emergency medical technicians, and emergency room doctors and nurses) is a noble calling. Their jobs often require them to see humanity at its worst, and they are expected urgently to address and fix the many terrible and ugly things that people can do to each other or themselves. Society expects those first responders to carry the heavy burden of virtue. Their families share in that burden. That burden can be generally unspoken as revealed readily by some of the following statistics. Between 9/11 (September 11, 2001) and May 2021, approximately 30,177 active-duty personnel and veterans of the post- 9/11 wars died by suicide. That obscene and tragic number is more than four times the number of military personnel killed in military operations, including training accidents. In 2019, more law enforcement officers died by suicide than by felonious killings or accidental deaths in the line of duty. In 2018, firefighters died at higher suicide rates than police officers—and firefighter suicides exceeded the rate of on-duty deaths by approximately 30%. Healthcare first responders aren’t spared from these gruesome statistics. Even leaving aside the devastating effects of the COVID pandemic, emergency room doctors and nurses, and emergency medical technicians, face significantly higher suicide risks than members of the general population. Like his first responder brothers and sisters, Mitch was all about public service. In Piedmont, he earned the rank of Eagle Scout, received the Public Service Award from his high school graduating class, and served as a Sergeant in the city’s Police Explorer program. He received multiple Presidential Volunteer Service Awards from the President of the United States. Mitch’s Eagle Scout project benefitted the Oakland Police Department’s K-9 officers. Mitch turned down college admission because he wanted to start serving his country right away. He honorably served for four years in the United States Marine Corps, where he was an infantryman and a Combat Marksmanship Coach. He served seven months of that enlistment overseas. When he died, he was serving as a police officer in Arizona. Recognizing the outsized role that first responders play in our society and that society owes them much more than they receive, the Mitch Winters First Responders Foundation provides annual grants to children of first responders in Alameda County. Through donations and support from the public, the foundation grants may be used for trade school (which Mitch thought society undervalued), community college, college or university, or graduate school. Applications are due November 30, and successful applicants will be notified on January 31. For more information about the foundation, including how to donate and how to apply, visit https://mitchwintersfirstrespondersfoundation.org/. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223

articles.text: Construction of a new house or a remodel of an existing house can be a long drawn-out and stressful process. What can one do to improve the likelihood that a construction project is a successful one? Who you hire to guide you through the project can have a big impact on reducing the stress and unpredictability of any given project. Another aspect of the process that can make a big difference in the results one achieves is to initially engage in a thoughtful and thorough design process, and then develop and document the design in sufficient detail to create a clear road map for construction. Contrary to Robert Burns’ statement, “The best-laid plans of mice and men often go awry”, I have always found that the best laid plans actually make for a more successful project. It is so important in any construction project to have a thoroughly thought-out design that has been studied carefully. This involves looking at multiple design iterations of different ideas. There is nothing more disruptive and expensive than second guessing a plan in the middle of a construction project. Shifting gears during construction can often end up being very expensive and most likely extend the construction schedule. The extra time and effort looking at various design options at the start makes for a more confident process moving forward. Once a general design has been settled upon, after careful study of various ideas, the selected design approach needs to be developed three dimensionally. The three-dimensional aspects should be considered during the two-dimensional layout but then fleshed out after one preferred layout has been selected. All design considerations, interior and exterior, should be thoughtout thoroughly in tandem. What I have described above are the ‘design phases’ of the project. Once the preliminary design and the design development phases are complete, more detailed drawings for the regulatory agencies as well as for the execution of construction need to be developed. I like to make the case that the design process doesn’t really end until the project has been completely constructed, because during this phase of the work, many detail decisions that may affect the design are made and imbedded in the construction drawings. The more care and thought one has applied to these design decisions and then documented properly, the better the road map for construction. Again, to my way of thinking, there is nothing like the best laid plans. articles.text: Piedmont Seniors pose in front of a stunning floral display at the Ritz Carleton Hotel in Half Moon Bay during a special group tour of this luxurious site. On a delightful fall day in October, the Piedmont Seniors made an excursion to the beautiful coastside town of Half Moon Bay. Usually, the town is overcast and foggy, but the Seniors lucked out and the weather was beautiful. The Seniors decided to take the scenic route, going from San Francisco to Pacifica to Highway 1 on the coast instead of the more common route on Highway 92 through San Mateo. Back in the day the small towns along the coast were popular with bootleggers during Prohibition, where alcohol could be secretly delivered to coastal restaurants with little chance of being caught. The Seniors’ first stop was the luxurious Ritz Carleton Hotel, located on a bluff of Half Moon Bay overlooking the Pacific Ocean, located approximately 30 minutes from both San Francisco and San Jose. It truly was a highlight of the day to see the elegant resort up close. The Ritz Carlton is proud of merging luxury with nature and has fire pits, two 18 hole golf courses, including one designed by Arnold Palmer! The hotel is known for its spa treatments as well as outstanding dining at the Navio Restaurant, which is rated one of the top brunches in Northern California. As the Seniors entered the hotel lobby, they saw a large, sumptuous pink silk flower display to acknowledge breast cancer awareness month. The group was given a private tour of the property, inside and out. The hotel hosts numerous weddings and social events due to its beautiful location on the ocean. The Seniors next explored the historic, quaint downtown of Half Moon Bay, where some of the brave souls visited the town’s jail. The jail once housed local lawbreakers in its two small cells. Today it houses the Half Moon Bay Coastside History Museum, telling the story about the Ohlone Indians, the first Coastsiders, Spanish and Mexican eras, the California Gold Rush, the Prohibition Era, and World War II. There are historians available for tours, with advance notice. The town is incredibly busy during weekends in October due to the many fields of pumpkins and the well known pumpkin weighing contest, along with rides and special events for children. The Seniors then had a delicious lunch in the heart of Main Street at Fattoriaemare, an authentic Italian restaurant with inside and outside seating. After lunch the Seniors headed to Pastorino Farms, one of the many nurseries on the outskirts of town on highway 92. They had a field of pumpklns from which to choose, along with gift items, plants and cut flowers. Some of the Seniors opted to take a short train ride around the property. On weekends in October, they offer a haunted house, face painting, hay rides, ponies, and opportunities to feed farm animals. Just a short walk away is Half Moon Bay Lavender Farm and Half Moon Bay Nursery, also with enticing gifts and, of course, more pumpkins. The Seniors couldn’t have asked for a more perfect day to celebrate this year’s Fall season. To find out more about the Piedmont Seniors meetings and their activities, contact Janet Epstein, the group’s coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Suffering from life-threatening health issues, a bear cub is now undergoing rehabilitation efforts at Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. An orphaned black bear cub, estimated to be eight months old and weighing 28 pounds, was brought to Oakland Zoo on Friday night, November 11, by wildlife biologists from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW). The cub is suffering from multiple health issues, including a severe skin infection that has caused extreme hair loss, pneumonia, a viral infection, internal parasites, and a deeply infected bone in his left front foot, causing lameness in walking. The cub was named “Nixon” by the concerned citizens who reported him wandering into a retail shop called Nixon in South Lake Tahoe last week. CDFW received the cub from the Bear League in Lake Tahoe after the group posted a story about the bear on its Facebook page. CDFW conducted a veterinary assessment treatment, performed initial examinations, and contacted Oakland Zoo for further care and hopeful rehabilitation at the Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. “It’s touch and go right now. This cub is a tough little guy; despite his physical state, he’s eating well and is in good spirits,” said Dr. Alex Herman, Head of Veterinary Services at Oakland Zoo. “We are putting our best efforts into practicing next-level medicine on him, and hope we can save his life.” Nixon has been receiving treatment at the Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital since his arrival, and on Tuesday morning, November 15, underwent an extensive medical examination by the Zoo’s veterinary team. Bloodwork was sent to several labs, x-rays, an ultrasound, dermatology assessment, dental exam, and more were also completed during the hours-long medical procedure. Currently, his prognosis is extremely guarded, but hopeful. Nixon is being administered antibiotics, antifungals, and special baths to treat his infected skin. Due to his lack of fur, he’s being kept warm by heat lamps at the veterinary hospital and being fed a special diet of “bear chow” soaked in formula, various produce, and browse. Oakland Zoo’s veterinary team will continue to monitor him daily and alter his treatment as needed. The primary concern is the infected bone in his foot and his severe pneumonia. An orphaned black bear cub, estimated to be eight months old and weighing 28 pounds, was brought to Oakland Zoo on Friday night, November 11, by wildlife biologists from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW). The cub is suffering from multiple health issues, including a severe skin infection that has caused extreme hair loss, pneumonia, a viral infection, internal parasites, and a deeply infected bone in his left front foot, causing lameness in walking. The cub was named “Nixon” by the concerned citizens who reported him wandering into a retail shop called Nixon in South Lake Tahoe last week. CDFW received the cub from the Bear League in Lake Tahoe after the group posted a story about the bear on its Facebook page. CDFW conducted a veterinary assessment treatment, performed initial examinations, and contacted Oakland Zoo for further care and hopeful rehabilitation at the Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. “It’s touch and go right now. This cub is a tough little guy; despite his physical state, he’s eating well and is in good spirits,” said Dr. Alex Herman, Head of Veterinary Services at Oakland Zoo. “We are putting our best efforts into practicing next-level medicine on him, and hope we can save his life.” Nixon has been receiving treatment at the Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital since his arrival, and on Tuesday morning, November 15, underwent an extensive medical examination by the Zoo’s veterinary team. Bloodwork was sent to several labs, x-rays, an ultrasound, dermatology assessment, dental exam, and more were also completed during the hours-long medical procedure. Currently, his prognosis is extremely guarded, but hopeful. Nixon is being administered antibiotics, antifungals, and special baths to treat his infected skin. Due to his lack of fur, he’s being kept warm by heat lamps at the veterinary hospital and being fed a special diet of “bear chow” soaked in formula, various produce, and browse. Oakland Zoo’s veterinary team will continue to monitor him daily and alter his treatment as needed. The primary concern is the infected bone in his foot and his severe pneumonia. articles.text: Miriam and Jerry Friedkin at home in Piedmont Gerald S. Friedkin, a Piedmont resident for 49 years, passed away peacefully at home from cancer on October 14 surrounded by his family. He was 79. Born on May 9, 1943, Jerry grew up in Oakland and graduated from Oakland High School in 1960. From an early age, Jerry took on all sorts of odd jobs – delivering the Oakland Tribune, distributing Kosher meat, working the night shift at the main post office, restoring used cars – which gave him a lifelong appreciation for hard work. After graduating from San Francisco State, Jerry built a successful real estate investment company and became known for his honesty and integrity. He loved the art of negotiation and generously mentored many young professionals. Jerry was a loyal and wise counselor to his family and friends. He nurtured lifelong relationships over many Shabbat dinners, rounds of golf, Sunday walks to Montclair, and Scotch happy hours in his backyard. Always welcoming and inclusive, Jerry was a builder of community. He served as president of Beth Jacob Congregation and the Jewish Foundation of the East Bay, co-founded the Oakland Hebrew Day School, and supported countless other organizations throughout the Bay Area and beyond. A quiet philanthropist and leader, he was a pillar of the East Bay Jewish community who lived his values of charity, kindness, and repairing the world. In addition to his wife of 51 years, Miriam, he is survived by his brothers Stephen (Terry) and Morton (Amy); his children Julie (Reuven Kahane), Ilana (Reed Bennett), Yael (Matthew Kovner) and David (Sarah Marder-Eppstein); and his grandchildren David, Gabriela, and Annika Kahane, Aaron, Ariana and Abigail Bennett, Eve and Jacob Kovner, and Noam Friedkin. Above all his many accomplishments, Jerry was a wonderful husband, father, brother and friend. As humble as he was generous, Jerry truly lived a life of meaning, purpose, and love. May his memory be a blessing. The family has established the Gerald S. Friedkin Memorial Fund (℅ JCF, 121 Steuart St, San Francisco, CA 94105) to receive charitable contributions friends may wish to make in his memory. Grants from this fund will support the causes that mattered most to Jerry.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group seems to be charmed when it comes to the weather. It had rained on Tuesday but was clear by the time the group assembled at the Exedra last Wednesday morning. It was great walking weather, and a strong turnout of 40 walkers showed up for a morning together. It was announced that Piedmont historian and walker Meghan Bennett has created a Walking on Wednesday website. It contains the stories of Walking on Wednesdays walks going back to group’s start in 2018 (https:// www.walkingpiedmont.com/). The group has a goal of walking every traffic-safe street in Piedmont each year, and has walked all but a few this year, including the upper parts of Palm and Nova Drives, as well as Dale Avenue and Sylvan Way. Getting to them would allow the group to walk through Piedmont Park, and see how much water was in Bushy Dell Creek after the recent rain. At the top of the park, behind the Community Hall, the group checked the water level in the creek. It was still good to see water flowing after the long. dry season and the drought we are experiencing. The group took the lower park trail to be closer to the creek, stopping at the cascades that Frank C. Havens built when he created the park in the 1890s as an attraction for his real estate sales. The stairs overlooking the cascades that provided tiers for the walkers to pose on for a group photo. The walkers continued on the path in a long line, and regrouped at the former sulphur spring grotto where Mark Twain visited the park in about 1868 during a writer’s tour and sampled the mineral water. Matt Gerhardt asked why there isn’t a sulphur smell now. It was explained that in the mid- 20th Century the neighbors didn’t like the smell, and had the City cap the spring. As the walkers went through the park, they had a pleasant surprise when they came upon former Piedmont Recreation supervisor Michael Murphy who was walking his dog. Emerging on Wildwood Avenue, they went past Wildwood School to the 5-W intersection of Wildwood, Wallace, Winsor and Warfield. They went down Winsor Avenue to Park View Drive, and then to the top of Palm Drive. There the story of Havens planting palm trees as a grand entrance to his park was also told. There are still some of Havens’ palm trees in people’s front yards, but most are now gone. The group went down Palm to Wildwood where it intersects with Sylvan Way and started its short by steep assent. The walkers seemed to enjoy the climb and the extra exercise it provided. They went down Sylvan to Boulevard Way and then past the office of the Piedmont Post near the corner of Grand Avenue. The walkers turned up Wildwood Avenue, past the Nova Circle, and came to the one-block, little-traveled Dale Avenue. From there it was on to Fairview, Jerome, and Oakland Avenues. A home on Oakland Avenue had Japanese maple trees with striking, beautiful red leaves. The street also provided another climb for the walkers before they came to the 300 block of El Cerrito Avenue. It is a level walk until Magnolia Avenue, which gave the group one last uphill challenge nefore arriving back at the Exedra. It turned out that all these hills and the almost a three mile walk were not that much of a challenge for the group. They have been climbing almost all of Piedmont’s streets all year long, and the walkers are confident they will finish the Turkey Trot route first in a couple of weeks on the day before Thanksgiving. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: On Monday, November 7th, fall weather finally arrived for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group. It was cool, so instead of meeting outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park, they moved inside the Piedmont Community Hall. There was an excellent turnout of 18 readers, including Dale Benveniste, Adrienne Hamlin, Sarah Johnson, Mike Henn, Mike Bandrowski, Jerry Gragg, Darby Gragg, Bob Hall, Martin Levy, Laura Goldman, Pat McMahon, Lois Price, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Carol Long and Priscilla Wanerus. Treats provided by Carol Long were largely from Japan to recognize Kazuo Ishiguro, the author of the group’s November selection, Klara and the Sun. It was published in 2021 and is science fiction. This is the eighth novel by the Nobel Prize-winning, British writer. Ishiguro’s story is set in the U.S. in an unspecified, dystopian future where some children are genetically engineered, or “lifted,” to enhance their academic ability. Schooling is provided entirely at home by on-screen tutors, so opportunities for socialization are limited and parents who can afford it often buy their children androids as companions. The book’s narrative is told by Klara, a solar-powered AF (Artificial Friend), who is chosen by Josie, a sickly, 14-year-old to be her companion. Josie lives with her mother in a remote region of prairie. Soon after joining them, Klara learns that the lifting process carries some risk. Josie’s older sister Sal had earlier died, and Josie herself is gravely ill. Josie’s only near neighbor and childhood friend is Rick, a boy of about her own age. Although academically able, Rick has not been lifted and faces discrimination and reduced career prospects. In spite of this, Josie and Rick have always known that they will be together forever. Although Klara is exceptionally intelligent and observant, her knowledge of the world is The prose and story development also disappointed them. Others found it simplistic, but still eloquent, creative, and cleaver. However the group did believe the book presented a possible future that their grandchildren may have to face. As machines become more like humans, it is a potential, scary future with moral questions that Ishiguro wants us to consider today. Klara and the Sun got the group thinking and talking about related issues. The questions of upper income parents providing extra tutoring for their college-aspiring children, and the appropriateness of the SAT exam and Affirmative Action in college admissions were also considered before the readers refocused on the book for some final thoughts. The group seemed to agree that Klara and the Sun was a worthwhile book to read, and it had been a good discussion. Ishiguro was able to make this science fiction future and Klara’s plight seem real for readers. Some found Klara’s being treated like a “vacuum cleaner” at the book’s end to be sad, and they were left with feelings of melancholy. The readers also agreed the moral issues Ishiguro raises are ones we should be thinking about now and working on solutions because our decedents may have to grapple with them in the not-too-distant future. With their discussion complete, the readers considered their next books. The group tries to alternate monthly between fiction and non-fiction books. They had previously selected the non-fiction Priestdaddy by Patricia Lockwood for December and Afterparties by Anthony Veasna So for January. After some consideration, the group picked Prisoners of Geography: Ten Maps that Explain Everything About the World, by Tim Marshall for their February read. The group’s next meeting will be Monday, December 5 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by calling the Recreation Department at 420- 3070. limited. Through an experience, Klara comes to believe that the sun has great kindness and a special kind of nourishment that can save Josie. The novel tells how Klara works to get the sun to help Josie regain her health, as Klara believes it can. Klara and the Sun generated a lot of discussion, which the group enjoyed. There were those who really enjoyed the book, and those that didn’t, with the former being in the majority. One reader felt the book was a “remarkable achievement” that contained many concepts and moral choices for the reader to contemplate. There was the relationship between humans and machines, the place of artificial intelligence in our society as it increases its power and dominance over human intellect, humans’ responsibilities to machines that contribute to our lives in personal ways, the development of religion to help make sense of the world, the importance of programming and misinterpretation of experience, the consequences of loneliness, and more. Ishiguro doesn’t answer the questions he raises, but rather leaves them for the reader to consider, interpret, discuss, and decide. There also were those who were not so enchanted with the book. Some said it was “junior fiction” that 9th graders would find interesting. It was a little long and dragged for some, and was like “the autobiography of a machine,” one said. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

This finding arose from the facts, cited in the EIR, that (1) Caltrans assumes a sight distance of 385 feet to allow vehicles traveling at 35 MPH to stop safely, (2) at least 15% of vehicles on Moraga Avenue at Blair Park exceeded 35 MPH, and (3) no location at Blair Park provided a 385-foot sight distance for drivers traveling in either direction. Building a footbridge seemed an intuitive solution to the sight-distance problem for pedestrians. As the EIR reported, however, experience with footbridges showed that pedestrians, particularly children, “dash” rather than use a bridge if opportunities to cross appear at street level. Footbridges reduced deaths only when a wall at street level forces pedestrians to cross on the bridge. A wall on Moraga Avenue was, however, thought ineffective because it would have had to include dash-inducing gaps for vehicular left turns into and out of Blair Park. A footbridge, moreover, would not have solved the sight distance problem for vehicles entering and exiting parking lots at Blair Park. Slowing vehicles on Moraga Avenue to the 25 MPH speed limit by enforcement, roundabouts, and road narrowing was considered in 2010. These options were rejected because they would have created a dangerous, rush-hour “back up” at the Highway 13/Moraga Avenue interchange which has a short sight distance for vehicles traveling south on Highway 13. Impeding traffic on Moraga would also have shifted travel to Oakland Avenue creating congestion and safety problems along its entire route through Piedmont. To assign 60 or more extremely and very low-income families to Blair Park would be not only dangerous but also uncivil. An extremely low-income neighborhood accessible only by a thoroughfare known unsafe for drivers and pedestrians would be, to say the least, stigmatized and isolated. This isolation would be made worse if, as is likely, parents rightly fearful of the unsafe conditions on Moraga Avenue, kept their children from visiting friends in Blair Park. Assigning extremely low-income families to Blair Park is not only unsafe and uncivil, but also unnecessary given the obviously better solution of integrating them into the new neighborhood of market-rate housing planned for the area around Coaches Field. The first draft of the Housing Element included 60 very and extremely low-income units in that neighborhood and showed no housing in Blair Park. We should return to that plan because it would tempt no one to cross Moraga Avenue. The Corporation Yard, which attracts no pedestrians and generates few vehicular trips, could be moved to Blair Park to make room, if needed, for added housing. Rather than becoming a segregated community, Piedmont could celebrate a new, safe, and inclusive neighborhood.

This finding arose from the facts, cited in the EIR, that (1) Caltrans assumes a sight distance of 385 feet to allow vehicles traveling at 35 MPH to stop safely, (2) at least 15% of vehicles on Moraga Avenue at Blair Park exceeded 35 MPH, and (3) no location at Blair Park provided a 385-foot sight distance for drivers traveling in either direction. Building a footbridge seemed an intuitive solution to the sight-distance problem for pedestrians. As the EIR reported, however, experience with footbridges showed that pedestrians, particularly children, “dash” rather than use a bridge if opportunities to cross appear at street level. Footbridges reduced deaths only when a wall at street level forces pedestrians to cross on the bridge. A wall on Moraga Avenue was, however, thought ineffective because it would have had to include dash-inducing gaps for vehicular left turns into and out of Blair Park. A footbridge, moreover, would not have solved the sight distance problem for vehicles entering and exiting parking lots at Blair Park. Slowing vehicles on Moraga Avenue to the 25 MPH speed limit by enforcement, roundabouts, and road narrowing was considered in 2010. These options were rejected because they would have created a dangerous, rush-hour “back up” at the Highway 13/Moraga Avenue interchange which has a short sight distance for vehicles traveling south on Highway 13. Impeding traffic on Moraga would also have shifted travel to Oakland Avenue creating congestion and safety problems along its entire route through Piedmont.
